core_idea: The condition is governed entirely by how many copies of the smallest relevant value, 0, are available. Zero copies make every MEX zero, one copy makes exactly one MEX positive and is impossible, while at least two copies can support two multisets with MEX 1 and leave the third with MEX 0.
key_observations: A multiset has positive MEX if and only if it contains 0.
If there are no zeroes, all three MEX values are 0, so the condition is automatically satisfied.

With exactly one zero, only one multiset can have positive MEX; the other two have MEX 0. Therefore the sum equals the maximum, which cannot be at least twice the maximum when that maximum is positive.
With at least two zeroes, two different multisets can each obtain MEX 1.
Once a multiset contains 0, its MEX is at least 1; assigning only one zero to it guarantees its MEX is exactly 1 regardless of which positive values it receives.
All non-zero elements can be placed in the third multiset without changing its MEX from 0.
reasoning_patterns: Identify a critical value whose presence determines whether the objective can become positive.
Reduce feasibility to the multiplicity of that critical value rather than analyzing the full value distribution.
Use extreme-case analysis to prove impossibility when a required resource is insufficient.
Construct a witness by assigning scarce critical resources to separate groups and placing irrelevant elements arbitrarily.
Force an exact small MEX by ensuring the critical prefix is partially present: include 0 but do not need to control larger values.
Compare the total objective with its maximum component to derive structural requirements on how many components must be positive.
questions: Which smallest value determines whether the objective is zero or positive?
How many groups must have a positive contribution?
What resource is needed to make multiple groups positive?
Can feasibility be characterized by the frequency of one critical value?
Can I force an exact small value instead of optimizing a larger one?
Which elements are irrelevant once the critical condition is satisfied?
What happens in the cases where the critical resource is absent, unique, or repeated?
